transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; what brings you in to see me today?

Nice to meet you, Dr. Smith. Well, what actually made me call the EAP is that... lately, I've been really jumpy. Every little bang in the office, like a file drawer shutting or someone dropping a coffee mug, it just makes me jump hard. And then my chest keeps racing for way longer than it probably should. It's been pretty distracting, so I figured I should come in and talk to someone about it.
Did these symptoms start following a specific, frightening, or life-threatening event?

Yeah, they did. Um, this has all been going on for about two weeks now. It started right after... well, I had this late-night confrontation with my regional boss. It got pretty intense, and ever since that happened, I've just been dealing with this.
Have you been having any unwanted memories or vivid dreams about that confrontation with your boss?

No, not really. I mean, I haven't had any nightmares about it or anything like that. And I'm not, you know, constantly replaying it in my head during the day either. It's just that jumpiness I mentioned.

Outside of the reactions you have to sudden noises, have you been feeling constantly worried or anxious about other aspects of your daily life, such as your work performance or personal responsibilities, for most of the past six months?

No, not really. Um, before this happened a couple of weeks ago, I was doing fine. I don't constantly worry about my work performance or my personal life, and definitely not for the last six months. It's really just been since that confrontation that I've been having these issues with being so jumpy. Other than that, my day-to-day stress is just the normal amount, I'd say.
Have these feelings of being 'jumpy' and the racing heart been making it difficult for you to complete your work tasks or interact with your coworkers?

Yeah, it has been making things difficult. I mean, I'm still making it to work every day, but I'm definitely slower when it comes to going over accounts and making staffing decisions. I've even had to ask my team to double-check things that I would normally just handle on my own. It's frustrating, and honestly, with performance reviews coming up soon, I'm pretty worried that these little mistakes and delays are going to end up affecting my job.
Beyond the jumpiness and racing heart, have you been feeling particularly sad, hopeless, or down since that confrontation?

No, not really. I wouldn't say I feel sad or hopeless. I mean, I'm definitely stressed out about falling behind and the upcoming reviews, but I don't feel down in that way. It's really just that physical on-edge feeling I get.
Would you say that the level of stress and anxiety you've been feeling since that confrontation is significantly more intense than what most people would typically experience in a similar situation?

I'm not really sure how to answer that. I mean, I guess I've never really been in a situation exactly like this before, so it's hard to compare. I just know that for me, it feels like a lot. I'm usually pretty level-headed, but right now, I just feel really wound up. I don't know if it's more than what someone else would feel, but it's definitely more than what I'm used to dealing with.
Do you feel that your current level of distress is causing you significant impairment in your social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning?

Like I mentioned a minute ago, it's really mostly affecting my job right now. I'm still showing up every day, but I'm just a lot slower when it comes to going through the accounts and making staffing decisions. Having to ask my team to double-check things that I usually handle completely on my own is definitely a setback for me. So yeah, it is causing some issues, especially since I'm pretty worried about how these mistakes and delays are going to look on my upcoming performance review. Outside of work, things are mostly normal, but professionally, it's definitely getting in the way.
Looking back at that confrontation with your boss, would you say that your level of distress is clearly out of proportion to the severity or intensity of the situation itself?

I mean, I don't really know if I'd call it out of proportion. It felt like a pretty severe situation to me at the time. He was really in my face, so... being this stressed about it feels somewhat justified, I guess? 

I just didn't expect the edge to linger this long. But looking back at how intense the actual argument was, I wouldn't say my reaction is completely crazy for what happened. I just wish I could shake it off faster.
Have you noticed any changes in your physical health since the confrontation, such as persistent muscle tension, difficulty falling or staying asleep, or frequent headaches?

Not really, no. I mean, my sleep has been pretty normal, and I haven't had any headaches or muscle tension that I've noticed. It's really just that mental edge I was talking about. But physically, I feel fine.
